# Part 1 — The case definition

## Target, source, analytic — and what each step costs

| Population | Here | Why it narrows |
|---|---|---|
| **Target** | adults with MASLD in the US | who we want to speak about |
| **Source** | NHANES 2007–2018 respondents | who was sampled |
| **Analytic** | those surviving every filter, with measurable exposure *and* outcome | who we can actually compute on |

- Each narrowing step trades **generalizability** for **measurability**
- A drop is not automatically a bias. **What it is depends on its kind** — Week 2's typed
  funnel: `ELIGIBILITY`, `DESIGN`, `MISSINGNESS`, `TARGET POPULATION`,
  `OUTCOME ASCERTAINMENT`
- Only one of those five is a missing-data problem

> Recall Week 2's measured check: adults in and out of the fasting subsample differ by
> **0.2 years, 0.02 kg/m², 0.07 cm**. Designed subsampling is *not* self-selection.

::: {.notes}
(6 min) Draw the nested circles if you like, but the labels on the arrows matter more than
the circles. Be careful here: an earlier version of this course taught every drop as a
preview of selection bias, and that was wrong — the measured balance in the blockquote is
why. The transferable habit is that the *kind* of each drop was checked rather than
assumed. We put the real typed funnel on screen after the break.
:::

## MASLD: a concept that has to become data operations

**MASLD** (formerly NAFLD) = **hepatic steatosis** + **metabolic dysfunction**, other
causes not dominant.

| Conceptual ingredient | What NHANES can offer | What the paper does |
|---|---|---|
| Hepatic steatosis | no biopsy, no imaging | **Fatty Liver Index ≥ 60** |
| Metabolic dysfunction | labs, exam, questionnaire | **≥ 1 of five** cardiometabolic criteria |

- The constraint is real, not a flaw in this paper: every NHANES population study of MASLD
  this decade faces it
- **Nobody in this dataset was diagnosed with MASLD.** There is no column to read. Who
  counts as a case is the output of a calculation you run yourself — four measurements,
  one published formula, one threshold
- So who is in the cohort depends on how you handle those inputs. Later today: one
  triglyceride value moves a single person in or out of the case definition, and one
  sentence of prose moves **2,063**

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Note the NAFLD→MASLD renaming so they recognise both terms in the literature. The
key move is the left-to-right one: a conceptual definition becomes a data operation, and
everything downstream inherits the properties of that operation. Do not let this land as
criticism. The last bullet makes two promises — the FLI boundary flip and the alcohol
sentence — and both are cashed later in the lecture; say them as promises so the room is
waiting for them.
:::

## Steatosis: the Fatty Liver Index, and where its inputs live

$$\mathrm{FLI} = 100 \cdot \frac{\exp(y)}{1+\exp(y)}, \qquad
y = 0.953\ln(\mathrm{TG}) + 0.139\,\mathrm{BMI} + 0.718\ln(\mathrm{GGT}) + 0.053\,\mathrm{waist} - 15.745$$

| Input | NHANES variable | Component | Fasting? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Triglycerides (mg/dL) | `LBXTR` | `TRIGLY` | **yes** |
| BMI (kg/m²) | `BMXBMI` | `BMX` | no |
| GGT (U/L) | `LBXSGTSI` | `BIOPRO` | no |
| Waist (cm) | `BMXWAIST` | `BMX` | no |

- Bedogni 2006. A published logistic score — **not** a product of the four
- **One** input needs a fasting lab, and that one input binds the whole index to the
  fasting subsample
- `BMXBMI` and `BMXWAIST` also build the *exposure*. Week 2 named that **structural
  dependence**; M1 dissects what it does to an estimate

> **Where do I actually get `LBXTR`?** The reproduction site carries the full
> **[NHANES variable map](https://ehsanx.github.io/SPPH604-2026W/reproduction/VARIABLE_MAP.html)**
> — component, cycle availability, CDC codebook link, and the line of our code that reads
> it. Use it for your own paper's variables too.

::: {.notes}
(5 min) This table is the same one they saw in Week 2 under Q2 — say so, so it reads as a
callback rather than new material. The fasting column is the new thing, and it is what the
feasibility argument later in the lecture turns on. Hold the structural-dependence point
at the level Week 2 set it: named, not diagnosed.
:::

## FLI, worked: one subject

A 52-year-old with **TG 150 mg/dL**, **BMI 28.5**, **GGT 30 U/L**, **waist 99 cm**:

| Term | Computation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| $0.953\ln(\mathrm{TG})$ | $0.953 \times \ln(150)$ | 4.775 |
| $0.139\,\mathrm{BMI}$ | $0.139 \times 28.5$ | 3.962 |
| $0.718\ln(\mathrm{GGT})$ | $0.718 \times \ln(30)$ | 2.442 |
| $0.053\,\mathrm{waist}$ | $0.053 \times 99$ | 5.247 |
| constant | | −15.745 |
| | **$y$** | **0.681** |

$$\mathrm{FLI} = 100 \cdot \frac{\exp(0.681)}{1+\exp(0.681)} = \mathbf{66.4} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{FLI} \ge 60 \;\Rightarrow\; \textbf{steatosis}$$

- Note **TG and GGT enter on the log scale** — a doubling of GGT is worth the same as a
  doubling of TG times 0.75, not twice the raw units

::: {.notes}
(6 min) Do the arithmetic on screen rather than describing it. Ask them which term is
doing the most work before you reveal the column — most will guess BMI, and it is waist.
The log terms are the reason the index is not a simple weighted sum of the four
measurements, and the reason you cannot eyeball who is over the cut.
:::

## The same subject, one lab value later

Change **only** the triglycerides — everything else identical:

| | TG | $y$ | FLI | Case? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Visit A | 150 mg/dL | 0.681 | **66.4** | **yes** |
| Visit B | 110 mg/dL | 0.385 | **59.5** | no |

**The cut flips at TG = 112.4 mg/dL**, holding BMI, GGT and waist fixed.

- **40 mg/dL of triglycerides is the entire difference between "case" and "not a case"** —
  nothing else about these two rows differs
- So the one input that forced the cohort into the fasting subsample is also the one that
  decides case status at the margin
- A **cut on a continuous score** manufactures a hard boundary. The same issue returns at
  the **BMI × WHtR 2×2**

::: {.notes}
(6 min) This is the slide that makes dichotomisation concrete rather than a slogan. Ask
what they would do about it — the honest answers are a sensitivity analysis at 55 and 65,
or keeping FLI continuous where the question allows. Neither is available to us here,
because the case definition is the paper's, not ours; that constraint is itself worth
naming. Flag that the 2×2 exposure has exactly the same property. **Sourcing note:** this
slide deliberately does *not* claim that fasting triglycerides vary by 40 mg/dL within a
person between visits. That is very likely true and it is not established by anything on
these slides — if you want to make it in the room, bring a citation, because "assert it
and move on" is precisely what we mark students down for.
:::

## Metabolic dysfunction: five criteria, and ≥ 1 is required

| # | Criterion | Operationalised as | Variables |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Adiposity | BMI ≥ 25, **or** waist > 94 cm (M) / > 80 cm (F) | `BMXBMI`, `BMXWAIST` |
| 2 | Glycaemia | glucose ≥ 100, **or** HbA1c ≥ 5.7, **or** diabetes dx, **or** on treatment | `LBXGLU`, `LBXGH`, `DIQ010`, `DIQ050`, `DIQ070` |
| 3 | Blood pressure | SBP ≥ 130, **or** DBP ≥ 85, **or** on treatment | `BPXSY1–4`, `BPXDI1–4`, `BPQ050A` |
| 4 | Triglycerides | TG ≥ 150, **or** on lipid treatment | `LBXTR`, `BPQ100D` |
| 5 | HDL | ≤ 40 mg/dL (M) / < 50 (F) | `LBDHDD` |

- **Five separate criteria, not four.** 4 and 5 are both lipids but they are coded,
  thresholded and sexed separately — collapsing them into "dyslipidaemia" is the wrong
  level of abstraction for something you have to write as code
- Every row hides a decision: *which threshold? treated counts as met? which variable?*
- In this cohort ≥ 1 is almost always met — it drops **2 people, 6,052 → 6,050**. Report
  it anyway; your paper's population may differ

*Analysis set: locked mortality-linked cohort, N = 6,048.*

::: {.notes}
(8 min) Give this the time. This table is the codebook-before-coding discipline in its
finished form, and it is what P1 asks them to produce for their own paper. The "five not
four" point is worth saying out loud: a student who codes from a bullet that says
"dyslipidaemia" writes one indicator where the definition needs two with different cuts
and different sex rules. The 6,052 → 6,050 number is reassuring here and dangerous as a
habit — a non-binding filter is still a reported filter.
:::

# Part 2 — Eligibility as executable logic

## Exclusions are scientific claims

- Every filter answers *"who is this study about?"* — so every filter needs a **stated
  rationale**, not just a line of code
- The reproducibility contract, in one rule:

```r
# Paper, Methods: eligibility stated as "aged > 18 years"
d <- filter(d, age >= 18)          # NOT what the sentence says — deliberate, see below
```

- A comment naming **the sentence you are implementing** lets an auditor trace every
  `filter()` back to the paper
- It also makes a **divergence visible instead of invisible**. NHANES age is an integer, so
  `> 18` means 19 and over; we keep everyone aged exactly 18
- Week 2 put **three** age rules on one slide — the lab's `>= 20`, the paper's `> 18`, our
  `>= 18`. Same variable, three studies
- The discipline is not to pick the right one. It is to **record which one you used**, so a
  reader can undo it. A reproduction that quietly adopts the other rule has destroyed its
  own evidence

::: {.notes}
(6 min) Reframe "exclusion criteria" from a chore list into a set of claims. Then use the
age rule as the smallest possible worked example of the comment rule: the sentence and the
code **disagree**, the comment is what makes that checkable, and the divergence is recorded
rather than harmonised. Do not let anyone leave thinking `>= 18` is a typo — it is a choice
we wrote down. The alcohol criterion two slides on is the same situation with no defensible
resolution available.
:::

## The sentence

The paper's Methods exclude significant alcohol consumption:

> ### "> 2 drinks/day (men), > 1 (women)"

Three things it does not say:

| | The question it leaves open |
|---|---|
| **Which variable?** | `ALQ130` (drinks per *drinking day*) or `ALQ120Q × ALQ120U` (frequency × quantity)? |
| **Per what?** | per drinking day, or averaged over all days? |
| **And the missing?** | people who did not answer — dropped, or kept? |

- `ALQ130` is **drinks on days you drink**. Applying a "per day" rule to it directly is a
  different rule from the one the sentence appears to state

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Read the criterion aloud, then sit in the silence for a second. Almost everyone
hears it as unambiguous on first pass — that reaction is the lesson. Take the three rows
one at a time and ask the room to answer each before you move on. If you have the paper
open, put its full Methods paragraph on screen alongside; the criterion above is the
operative clause as recorded in `reproduction_report.md` §2.
:::

## One sentence, three cohorts

| Reading | Implemented as | Removes | Analytic N | vs the paper's ≈ 6,300 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Crude** — `ALQ130` applied flatly | `ALQ130 > 2` (M) / `> 1` (F) | **2,063** | **4,308** | −1,992 |
| **Frequency-weighted** — average drinks/day | quantity × frequency ÷ reference period | **427** | **5,944** | −356 |
| **No effective exclusion** | — | **0** | **6,371** | **+71** |

::: {.incremental}
- A swing of **2,063 people** — a third of the cohort — from one sentence
- The published N and death count are **far more compatible with the third row** than with
  either of the others. We are not claiming 6,371 *is* 6,300 — the residual +71 is the gap
  we account for two slides from now
- So the results are most consistent with the exclusion **not having been applied as we can
  operationalise it**. The Methods state it; the numbers do not show it
:::

*Analysis set: full reconstructed analytic file, N = 6,371.*

::: {.notes}
(10 min) The centre of the lecture — spend the time. Vote before revealing: which reading
would you defend? Take a count on each row. Then reveal the third row and let the
implication land: the ambiguity is invisible until you try to *run* it, and running it here
turned up something stronger than ambiguity. Resist supplying the resolution; there isn't
one available from the paper. This is the slide that motivates "never tune to hit the N".
:::

## The trap inside the trap: reserved codes

`ALQ130` uses NHANES **reserved codes**, not measurements:

| Code | Means |
|---|---|
| `777` | refused |
| `999` | don't know |

```r
qty <- ifelse(ALQ130 %in% c(777, 999), NA, ALQ130)   # strip BEFORE any threshold
```

- Left in, `ALQ130 > 2` silently reclassifies every refusal as a heavy drinker
- Here that is **nine people**: the crude exclusion moves **2,063 → 2,072**
- Two traps live on one variable and they are **two hundred times apart in size**. Do not
  fuse them in your notes

> A reserved code is not a quantity. Strip them before every threshold rule, in every
> increment.

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Small numbers, large principle. The nine people do not change any estimate, and
that is exactly why this is worth teaching: it is a wrong implementation that survives the
result-didn't-move defence. Say explicitly that the 2,000 belongs to the drinks-per-
drinking-day trap and the nine belongs to the reserved codes — an earlier version of this
course fused them and was wrong by a factor of two hundred.
:::

## What we did, and why we are telling you

**Our choice:** no effective alcohol exclusion. It reproduces the published cohort and is
the most transparent about the discrepancy.

```r
## 02_build_analytic.R:40
APPLY_ALCOHOL_EXCL <- FALSE
```

- It is a **switch**, not a hidden default: the funnel prints
  `Alcohol exclusion applied = FALSE` as a row, so the setting is in the artifact
- We carry the alcohol question forward as an **open finding**, not a solved step
- The discipline, stated once: **choose a priori, record the choice where a reader will
  find it, and report what the alternatives would have given**

> We are not telling you which reading is right. We are showing you what it costs to
> pretend the question did not arise.

::: {.notes}
(8 min) This is the slide the previous version of the deck was missing, and it is the one
that makes the previous three honest: we asked them to publish their coding decision, so
here is ours, in the code, with the alternatives quantified. Point out that the switch
appears as a row in the funnel — a decision recorded in the artifact cannot be forgotten by
the next person to run it. Ask what their own paper's equivalent switch is going to be.
:::

# Part 3 — The funnel

## The funnel, with a type on every row

| Step | Criterion | N | Dropped | Kind |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | NHANES 2007–2018 records | 59,842 | — | — |
| 1 | Age ≥ 18 | 36,580 | 23,262 | `ELIGIBILITY` |
| 2 | In fasting subsample | 14,962 | 21,618 | `DESIGN` |
| 3 | FLI computable | 14,170 | 792 | `MISSINGNESS` |
| 4 | Steatosis (FLI ≥ 60) | 6,052 | 8,118 | `TARGET POPULATION` |
| 5 | MASLD (≥ 1 criterion) | 6,050 | 2 | `TARGET POPULATION` |
| 6 | Phenotype group assignable | 6,050 | 0 | `MISSINGNESS` |
| 7 | Mortality-eligible and linked | **6,048** | 2 | `OUTCOME ASCERTAINMENT` |

- This is not a picture of the funnel. It **is** the funnel — emitted by
  `02_build_analytic.R` to `logs/sample_funnel.csv`, and re-derivable by anyone
- Report **removed *and* remaining** on every line. A lone final N is not reproducible

*Analysis set: locked mortality-linked cohort, N = 6,048.*

::: {.notes}
(9 min) Put this on screen and leave it there. Walk the type column, not the N column —
the Ns are arithmetic, the types are the analysis. Row 2 is the one to dwell on: the second
largest drop in the whole table is a *design* feature with a documented fix
(`WTSAF2YR`), not missing data to impute away. Row 3 is the genuine missingness, and it is
792 people, not 21,618. This is the artifact P1 asks them to produce.
:::

## Two row sets, and they are not interchangeable

| | Locked domain | Full analytic file |
|---|---|---|
| Fasting subsample enforced as its own step | **yes** (row 2) | fused into "FLI computable" |
| Final N | **6,048** | **6,371** |
| What it is for | every design-aware analysis; carries `WTSAF2YR` | matching the paper's reported cohort |
| Phenotype groups | — | 391 / 4,585 / 787 / 608 |
| Deaths | — | 586 |

- The paper reports **≈ 6,300**, groups **386 / 4,541 / 769 / 604**, **585 deaths** —
  those are *theirs*, and ours are the row above
- Quoting an N without naming its row set is the error this course exists to catch

> Two numbers that differ by 323 people are not a discrepancy if they are answers to
> different questions. They are a discrepancy if you never say which question.

::: {.notes}
(7 min) Read the two columns as two different objects, not as a right answer and a near
miss. Then read the paper's row separately, and say the group counts out loud in pairs
(386/391, 4,541/4,585, 769/787, 604/608) so that when these anchors reappear in the
survival weeks nobody hears ours as theirs. The habit being built is the row-set label,
which every quantitative slide in this course carries.
:::

## What the funnel reveals

- The single largest drop is **age ≥ 18** — 23,262 people. That is the study's own
  eligibility rule working as intended
- **After eligibility**, the two largest drops are the **fasting subsample** (21,618,
  `DESIGN`) and the **disease definition** (8,118, `TARGET POPULATION`)
- **Neither of those is missing data.** The genuine missingness in this table is 792 + 0
- Within the fasting subsample, FLI is computable for **94.7%** of adults

> Feasibility, before you commit: *is the exposure computable for enough of your target
> population?* Here the answer arrives as a design fact, not a data-quality problem.

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Keep the scoping exact — "after eligibility" — because the unscoped version of
this sentence is false against the table directly above it, and the printed drops are there
so a student can check rather than trust. This is also the answer to the feasibility
question they should be asking of their own locked paper today.
:::

## Why you never tune the cohort to hit the paper's N

- The temptation: quietly flip a threshold until N matches the abstract
- That is **fitting the process to the answer** — you have chosen your method using the
  result, and the method no longer carries evidence
- One sentence in this paper moves N by **2,063**. So an exact match is roughly as likely
  to mean *you guessed their ambiguity correctly* as *you implemented it correctly*

| | What it demonstrates |
|---|---|
| Matched N, undocumented coding | nothing — the match is unattributable |
| Mismatched N, traced to a named step | the reproduction worked |

> A documented N you can defend beats a matched N you cannot.

::: {.notes}
(7 min) The methodological heart of the reproduction philosophy, and it follows directly
from the alcohol slide rather than being asserted. Reframe success explicitly: at M1, a
gap you can trace to a specific decision scores above a match you cannot explain. The
grading criteria say so.
:::

## Reviewing someone else's eligibility

| Ask | On this paper |
|---|---|
| Is the case definition **operational**? | mostly — FLI ≥ 60 is exact; "≥ 1 criterion" needs the five spelled out |
| Is every exclusion **executable** as written? | **no** — the alcohol criterion is not |
| Does the funnel's arithmetic **close**? | not reported; we had to rebuild it |
| Is the analytic N **stated and reproducible**? | stated; reproducible only up to the above |

- Also check the tables against the Methods: here the Table 1–2 headers read **"BMI < 25"**
  while the Methods define obesity at **≥ 30**, and the non-obese groups have BMI medians
  of **27.6** and **28.8** — so the headers appear to be a labelling error
- **Charity and rigour together:** assume competence, and still require that the numbers
  reconcile

::: {.notes}
(6 min) This is the stance they bring to M2 and to their own defence at M3. The BMI header
is the cleanest small example in the course of a typographic slip with real consequences —
a reproducer who codes to 25 does not reproduce the groups. Note the hedge "appear to be":
we report what we can check, and we do not diagnose intent.
:::

# Part 4 — Thursday

## L2 assembles the same object from a different paper

EpiMethods [`accessingE2`](https://ehsanx.github.io/EpiMethods/accessingE2.html) —
**benzodiazepine / opioid use and all-cause mortality**, NHANES 1999–2014.

```r
dat.mort   <- rbind(dat.mortality99, dat.mortality01, ..., dat.mortality13)
dat.nhanes <- rbind(dat.nhanes99,    dat.nhanes01,    ..., dat.nhanes13)

dat <- merge(dat.mort, dat.nhanes, by = "SEQN", all = TRUE)
```

- **Eight cycles stacked, then merged on `SEQN`** — the same key and the same pattern L1
  used with `full_join(demo, bmx, by = "SEQN")`
- `all = TRUE` is the `full_join` decision again, made with a different word. Week 2's
  rule stands: **the join verb defines the analysis set**
- Mortality is a **separate linked file** here too — it is not an NHANES component

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Open with the fact that the lab is a different paper, so nobody is waiting for
MASLD to appear. Then show that the first move is identical to L1's and ask them what
`all = TRUE` does to the row set — they answered this exact question in Week 2 about
`full_join` versus `inner_join`.
:::

## And L2 writes a funnel — it just does not know it yet

```r
dat1 <- subset(dat,  RIDAGEYR >= 20)                            # N = 43,793
dat2 <- subset(dat1, RIDSTATR == "int + mec exam")              # N = 41,659
dat3 <- subset(dat2, TAKERX_INLASTMONTH %in% c("No", "Yes"))    # N = 41,614
dat4 <- dat3[complete.cases(dat3$BPQ020), ]                     # N not recorded
dat5 <- subset(dat4, mortstat == 0 | (mortstat == 1 & permth_int > 12))  # N = 31,591
dat6 <- subset(dat5, benzodiazepines == "Yes" | ssris == "Yes" | opioids == "Yes")  # N = 4,049
```

- Six eligibility steps, **N after each one** — that is a funnel, written as comments
- Now type it, the way we typed ours:

| | `dat1` | `dat2` | `dat3` | `dat4` | `dat5` | `dat6` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| kind | `ELIGIBILITY` | `DESIGN` | `MISSINGNESS` | `MISSINGNESS` | `ELIGIBILITY` | `TARGET POPULATION` |

- **`dat4` prints no N.** The complete-case steps are the ones that go uncounted — in this
  lab and in most papers

::: {.notes}
(7 min) The payoff slide for the whole lecture. They are looking at a real funnel in the
wild, in the crudest possible form: a numbered chain with N in comments. Ask the room to
supply the type row before you reveal it — arguing about whether `dat2` is design or
missingness is exactly the right argument. Then point at `dat4`: the step with no number is
the complete-case step, which is the one most likely to be doing quiet work. That is the
habit P1 is testing.
:::

## One more thing to notice on Thursday

L2's exposure has four levels, and the reference category is **"Neither"**:

```r
dat6 <- subset(dat5, benzodiazepines == "Yes" | ssris == "Yes" | opioids == "Yes")
dat6$exposure <- relevel(dat6$exposure, ref = "Neither")
```

- Eligibility required **at least one** of three drug classes. So "Neither" means *neither
  benzodiazepines nor opioids* — **everyone in it is an SSRI user**
- The reference group is an **active comparator**, not an unexposed population
- Exactly the shape of our Group I: every hazard ratio in the MASLD paper is measured
  against a group that is **obese**

> A ratio without its referent means nothing — and in both studies the referent is not
> "healthy".

::: {.notes}
(4 min) This is the best transfer point in the two studies and it is easy to miss in the
lab, so plant it now. The eligibility rule and the reference category are the *same
decision* seen twice: who you let into the cohort determines what your comparison can
mean. Week 2 made this point about Group I; here it is again in a completely different
paper, which is the evidence that it is a general property rather than a quirk.
:::

## P1 — the same two things, on your paper

- **Rebuild the cohort** from raw source files: list every file and cycle, name the merge
  key, write each inclusion and exclusion as **executable logic with a comment citing the
  sentence**
- **Produce the funnel**: N removed and N remaining at every step, typed
- **Flag one ambiguous eligibility sentence** you had to adjudicate — and say what the
  alternatives would have given
- Look variables up in the
  **[NHANES variable map](https://ehsanx.github.io/SPPH604-2026W/reproduction/VARIABLE_MAP.html)**
  rather than guessing: it says which cycles a variable exists in, and whether `77` is a
  code or a measurement
- **Do not aim at a number.** The paper reports ≈ 6,300; our full analytic file lands on
  6,371; yours is wherever your documented steps take you
- P1 is **optional and ungraded** — no deadline, nothing to submit. Keep the script, the
  flow table and `P1_notes.md` in your group repo. It is assembled into **M1**

> Be ready for: *"show me one person who is in your cohort but not the paper's — and tell
> me why."*

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Make the handoff crisp. L2 is the guided mechanics on a neutral paper; P1 is the
same mechanics plus today's judgment, on theirs. The M3 question in the blockquote is the
real standard — it cannot be answered from a final N, only from a funnel.
:::

## Where we landed

- Q2 answered all the way down: a **conceptual** case definition became an **operational**
  one, and the operations turned out to be **contestable**
- A cut on a continuous score decides case status at the margin; a five-criterion
  definition hides five threshold choices; one prose sentence yields **three cohorts**
- The funnel with a type on every row is what makes any of it checkable
- **Thursday:** the same assembly, a different paper. If you can only do it on MASLD, you
  have not learned it

*Reading a Methods section is the first act of reproduction. Building the cohort is the
second.*

::: {.notes}
(2 min) Close on the transfer claim, not on MASLD. Ask on the way out: what is the one
sentence in your own locked paper that you already suspect will not survive being written
as code?
:::
